a: These events took place
p: The opening formula is common in biblical stories. The rabbis heard a warning in it.
b: The Hebrew opens vayhi bimei, "And it happened in the days of," the same words that begin Ruth and that open stories in Genesis 14:1 and, in a close form, Judges 19:1. Like Ruth, Esther presents itself as a story set in the past, told to later readers. The Talmud notes that wherever Scripture opens this way, trouble follows: famine in Ruth's day, Haman in Esther's (Bavli Megillah 10b). The phrase also signals that, though Esther stands among the Writings in the Hebrew Bible, it is told as a historical narrative like the books before it.

a: This was the Ahasuerus
p: Almost all scholars identify him with Xerxes I, who ruled Persia from 486 to 465 BC.
b: The Hebrew name Achashverosh is a close rendering of the Old Persian Xshayarsha, which the Greeks wrote Xerxes; Babylonian documents spell it Ahshiyarshu. The same king appears in Ezra 4:6. Xerxes I fits the book's details: his empire reached India and Cush, he ruled from Susa and Persepolis, and Greek writers describe his lavish court and temper. The Greek Esther and Josephus call him Artaxerxes (see the variant), so some older writers thought of Artaxerxes I or II. The repeated "This was the Ahasuerus who ..." sounds like a storyteller distinguishing a famous king of the past, which many scholars take as a sign that the book was written some time after his reign.

a: from India all the way to Cush
p: Xerxes' own inscriptions list India and Cush (Nubia) as the edges of his empire.
b: Hoddu is the land of the Indus River (today's Pakistan), not all of India, and Kush is the land south of Egypt, the Nubia of modern Sudan, which older English Bibles call Ethiopia. A foundation text of Xerxes from Persepolis lists both among the lands he ruled, and Herodotus describes Indians and Ethiopians in his army. The "127 provinces" (medinot) are not the twenty or so great satrapies Herodotus lists but smaller districts within them; Daniel 6:1 speaks of 120 satraps. Some readers take the number as storytelling exaggeration; others as a real count of districts. The Old Greek has only "from India, 127 provinces," without Cush; the Alpha Text has "from India to Ethiopia" (see the variant).

a: the fortress at Susa
p: Susa was the Persian kings' winter capital. Its palace stood on a raised, walled mound.
b: On Susa and the word birah, see Nehemiah 1:1. Esther uses "the fortress at Susa" for the royal mound with its palace and harem, and "the city of Susa" for the town below (3:15). French excavations uncovered the great audience hall (apadana) of Darius I, which an inscription says Artaxerxes II restored after a fire. The book's descriptions of courts, gates and gardens have been compared with the site; how closely they match is debated. On whether Persian kings really sat "on the throne of" their kingdom at Susa in this period, see the chapter page.

a: his servants
p: Hebrew eved means servant or slave. Here it means the king's courtiers.
b: Avadim covers everyone who serves a master, from a field slave to a high minister. In Esther it means the king's courtiers and officials (1:3; 2:18; 3:2), so this site renders it "servants." Even the greatest of them were the king's servants in a real sense: their lives depended on his will, as Vashti, Haman and Esther all learn.

a: In his third year as king
p: The third year of Xerxes was 483 BC, a few years before his invasion of Greece.
b: Herodotus says that Xerxes, after putting down a revolt in Egypt, called together the leading Persians to plan the invasion of Greece (Histories 7.8). Some readers link the 180-day display (1:4) to that council: a long gathering of commanders, "the forces of Persia and Media," before the campaign of 480 BC. The book itself says nothing of Greece. Between this feast and Esther's crowning in the seventh year (2:16) the Persians lost the battles of Salamis (480) and Plataea (479). Those who read Esther as a story rather than a chronicle note that the dates serve its plot more than any campaign.

a: held a feast
p: Mishteh, a 'drinking,' is a feast. Esther has ten of them, and the plot turns at feasts.
b: The word comes from shatah, "drink." Esther has 20 of its 46 uses in the Bible. The king's two feasts (1:3–8) and Vashti's (1:9) open the book; Esther's crowning brings another (2:18); Haman and the king drink as the decree goes out (3:15); Esther's two feasts bring Haman down (5–7); and the Jews' feasting becomes Purim (9:17–19). Berlin and others see the book shaped around these pairs of feasts, and suited to a festival of eating and drinking.

a: porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl and colored stone
p: The cloths and stones of 1:6 are named with rare words. Several, including all four stones, are uncertain.
b: Karpas ("cotton") is a Persian loanword, akin to Sanskrit karpasa. Chur ("white") and tekhelet ("blue-violet") were the Persian royal colors: Mordecai later wears them (8:15). The four floor stones, bahat, shesh, dar, socheret, appear only here, and translators guess: porphyry or alabaster, marble, mother-of-pearl or pearl-colored stone, and a dark or patterned stone. The verse has no main verb in Hebrew, just a breathless list, as if the narrator is pointing around the hall. Glazed brick and stone floors of this kind have been found at Susa.

a: no two cups were alike
p: The rabbis imagined that the cups included the vessels taken from the Jerusalem Temple.
b: The Talmud (Bavli Megillah 11b–12a) and the Targums say that among the king's cups were the gold vessels Nebuchadnezzar took from the Temple, and that the Jews of Susa sinned by joining the feast. The idea comes from Daniel 5, where Belshazzar drinks from them, and from the claim that the king was celebrating the failure of Jeremiah's seventy years. Ezra 1:7–11 says Cyrus had already returned the vessels, and the Hebrew of Esther says nothing about them; the legend shows how Jewish readers filled the book's silence with meaning.

a: The drinking went by the law
p: Dat, a Persian loanword, appears about twenty times in Esther. Even the drinking has a law.
b: Dat (Old Persian data) means a royal law or order. It is the book's key word for the empire's power: a law for drinking (1:8), a law to punish Vashti (1:15), "the laws of Persia and Media" (1:19), laws that Haman says the Jews break (3:8), the law of death (3:14), the law that bars Esther from the king (4:11, 16), and finally a law for the Jews' defense (8:13). Many readers hear gentle mockery in a court that legislates even its drinking. Others see a contrast left unspoken: the book never mentions the law of Moses.

a: no one was to be pushed
p: It may mean guests did not have to drink when the king drank, or that there was no limit.
b: The Hebrew ein ones means "there is no forcing." The usual reading is that the normal court custom of drinking whenever the king drank was set aside, so each man drank as he liked. Others take it to mean no one was held back. Either way, the king's "law" here is about freedom to drink, an ironic start to a book in which his laws soon force a whole empire.

a: Vashti the queen
p: Greek sources name Xerxes' queen Amestris, not Vashti. How to fit the two is debated.
b: Herodotus names Amestris, daughter of the Persian noble Otanes, as Xerxes' wife and tells of her cruelty (Histories 7.61; 7.114; 9.108–113); the later Greek writer Ctesias makes her the mother of his successor Artaxerxes I. No source outside the Bible names Vashti or Esther. Some scholars argue that Vashti (perhaps Persian vahishta, "best") and Amestris could be forms of one name, or that Vashti was a wife other than the chief queen; others reply that Amestris was still queen mother long after Xerxes, so neither Vashti nor Esther could have been chief queen. Persian kings had several wives, and Herodotus says they took wives only from seven noble families (3.84), a rule the book ignores.

a: the seven eunuchs
p: Sarisim are court attendants. Many were castrated men, but the word can mean any court official.
b: The word goes back to Akkadian sha reshi, "he of the head," a royal attendant. Persian kings used castrated men to serve the women's quarters and the king's person, and Herodotus says eunuchs were prized as loyal (8.105). But the Hebrew word also names married officials such as Potiphar, "a court official of Pharaoh" (Genesis 39:1), so it does not always mean castration. In Esther, eunuchs carry every message between king and queen: Hegai, Shaashgaz, Hathach, Harbona and the would-be assassins (2:3, 14, 21; 4:5; 7:9). The Greek gives different names here, and one of them is Haman (Αμαν).

a: when wine had put the king in a happy mood
p: In Hebrew stories, a king or host whose heart is 'good with wine' is about to make a mistake.
b: The phrase is "when the king's heart was good with wine." Nabal's "heart was merry inside him" before he learned how near he had come to death (1 Samuel 25:36); Absalom waited until "Amnon's heart is feeling good with the wine" to have him killed (2 Samuel 13:28); and the Philistines' hearts were "good" (the site's Plain has "glad") when they called for Samson (Judges 16:25). Readers who know these stories expect trouble. The same mood brings Haman's ruin at Esther's feast of wine (5:6; 7:2).

a: in her royal crown
p: The text says she was to come wearing her crown. Rabbinic tradition said: wearing only her crown.
b: The Hebrew says Vashti was to come "in the royal crown" so the guests could see her beauty. The Talmud (Bavli Megillah 12b) and the Targums read it as "wearing only the crown," that is, naked, which would explain her refusal. Most modern commentators think that goes beyond the text: being shown off before a hall of drunken men was humiliating enough. Greek writers give mixed reports: Persian envoys in Herodotus say wives and concubines sat beside the men at Persian feasts (Histories 5.18), while Plutarch says the kings' wives left once the drinking began and only concubines stayed (Advice on Marriage 16). Josephus explains that Persian law forbade wives to be seen by strangers (Antiquities 11.191).

a: would not come
p: Readers have judged Vashti in opposite ways: wicked, foolish, modest, or brave.
b: The text gives no reason and no verdict. Rabbinic readers were mostly hard on her: the Talmud makes her Nebuchadnezzar's granddaughter, who forced Jewish girls to work naked on the Sabbath, and so was paid back in kind (Bavli Megillah 12b); others say she refused only because of a sudden blemish. Many traditional Christian readers saw her as a disobedient wife, rightly removed, and some sermons held her up as a warning; others praised her modesty. Feminist readers, from Elizabeth Cady Stanton's Woman's Bible (1898) on, have seen her as the book's first hero, a woman who would not be put on display, though some note she pays for it while Esther's quieter path saves her people. Many literary readers stress the comedy: the ruler of 127 provinces cannot rule his own wife. See the chapter page.

a: skilled in reading the times
p: It may mean astrologers, or experts in law and precedent.
b: "Knowing the times" can mean reading the stars for the right moment, as Babylonian and Persian court experts did, or knowing past cases and custom. The next words, "all who knew law and judgment," suggest legal experts. The same Hebrew describes men of Issachar "who knew how to read the times, and who knew what Israel ought to do" (1 Chronicles 12:32), where it means good judgment. The Talmud takes it as the rabbis, whom the king consulted (Bavli Megillah 12b).

a: the seven officials of Persia and Media
t: Seven nobles who saw the king's face
p: Persian tradition gave seven noble families special access to the king.
b: Herodotus tells how seven Persian nobles overthrew a usurper and agreed that each of them could enter the king's presence unannounced (Histories 3.84, 3.118). Ezra 7:14 speaks of Artaxerxes' "seven counselors." To "see the king's face" was a rare honor; the contrast is 4:11, where even the queen may not come before the king uncalled. The Greek gives only three names here, all different.

a: Memucan
p: The last-named adviser speaks first. The rabbis said he was Haman.
b: The Hebrew spells the name two ways here (written Mumcan, read Memucan), a spelling difference that does not change the sense. The Talmud says Memucan was Haman, "prepared" (mukan) for punishment (Bavli Megillah 12b), which makes Haman the man who removed Vashti and so, unwittingly, opened the way for Esther. Modern readers see no hint of this in the text, but the link shows how carefully the rabbis read the story's reversals. The Greek names him Mouchaios.

a: There will be more than enough scorn and anger
p: Memucan fears a wives' revolt across the empire. Many readers find the scene deliberately funny.
b: Memucan turns one wife's refusal into a threat to every husband from India to Cush, and his remedy, a decree sent to every province in every language (1:22), will spread the news far wider than gossip could. Many scholars read the chapter as satire of the Persian court: drunk, lavish, ruled by protocol and wounded pride (Fox; Berlin; Levenson). Traditional readers more often see a sober picture of a dangerous king whose moods become laws. Both readings agree that the scene sets the pattern for chapter 3, where another adviser turns a personal slight into an empire-wide decree.

a: the laws of Persia and Media, never to be undone
t: A law that cannot pass away
p: Esther and Daniel say Persian laws could not be revoked. No Persian source says so.
b: The phrase is literally "and it will not pass away." Daniel 6:8, 12 and 15 speak in the same way of a law of Media and Persia that does not pass away. No Persian text states such a rule, and Persian kings did change their orders. The Greek historian Diodorus tells of Darius III, who regretted an execution but could not undo it (Library 17.30), which shows the idea of a king bound by his own word. Whether it was a legal rule or a storytelling device, it matters for the plot: Haman's decree cannot be cancelled, only answered by a second decree (8:8).

a: a neighbor of hers who is better than she
p: The words echo Samuel's sentence on Saul, the Benjaminite king who spared Agag.
b: Memucan's phrase matches what Samuel told Saul after he spared Agag, king of Amalek: "Today the LORD has ripped Israel's kingship off you and given it to a neighbor of yours who is better than you" (1 Samuel 15:28). In Hebrew the two sentences share the rare expression "to your neighbor, the good one, more than you." Esther is about to be that "neighbor," and she is of Saul's tribe, Benjamin (2:5), facing "Haman ... the Agagite" (3:1). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, think the echo is deliberate: the story picks up where Saul failed. Others think the phrase was simply a common idiom.

a: to speak his own people's language
p: An obscure clause. It may mean the husband's language was to be spoken in a mixed household.
b: In a multilingual empire, a man might marry a woman of another people. The clause may mean the household was to use the husband's language, a sign of who ruled it. Compare Nehemiah's complaint that the children of mixed marriages "could not speak Judean; they spoke the tongue of this people or that" (Nehemiah 13:24). Other scholars think the text is damaged here: by changing a few letters it can read "and say whatever suits him." The Greek has a different clause (see the variant). Many readers find the edict absurd: no law can make a wife honor her husband.

a: and of the ruling made against her
p: The passive 'the ruling made against her' may hint that the king wished it undone.
b: The king remembers what Vashti did and "the ruling made against her," as if someone else had made it. Many readers hear regret: the law cannot be changed (1:19), and his advisers hurry to distract him with a new plan. Later Jewish retellings expand this into anger at the advisers who had urged him on. Others read the verse more simply: once his anger cooled, the king noticed he had no queen.

a: The king should name agents in each province of his kingdom
p: The proposal sounds like Joseph's advice to Pharaoh. Esther often echoes the Joseph story.
b: Joseph told Pharaoh, "let him appoint overseers over the land" and "Have them gather" what was needed (Genesis 41:34–35), and "Pharaoh liked the proposal" (Genesis 41:37), as the king does here (2:4). The two stories share more: a Hebrew in a foreign court who hides his identity, a reward for loyalty written into the record, a ring given by the king (Genesis 41:42; 3:10), a royal robe and a public ride (Genesis 41:42–43; 6:11), and a rise to second place in the kingdom (Genesis 41:43; 10:3). Scholars since the 1890s have listed these links; most think the writer of Esther modeled the story on Joseph's.

a: the house for the women
p: The royal harem was a closed household of wives, concubines and attendants under eunuch keepers.
b: Greek writers describe large Persian royal harems with hundreds of concubines (Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 27). The book describes two houses: one where the young women were prepared under Hegai (2:3, 8), and "the second women's house" for concubines under Shaashgaz (2:14). The women were "gathered" and "taken" (2:3, 8): they were not volunteers in a beauty contest, as the story is sometimes told, but young women taken into a king's household, most of whom would spend one night with him and then live out their lives as concubines.

a: a Jewish man
p: Yehudi first meant a man of Judah. Here a Benjaminite is called a Yehudi, a Jew.
b: This is the first time in the Bible that a man of another tribe is called Yehudi. In the Persian period the word had come to mean any member of the people who descended from the kingdom of Judah and worshiped its God, wherever they lived, not just the tribe of Judah: a Jew. Esther uses it more than any other book, and it is Mordecai's whole explanation for not bowing (3:4). The Talmud asks why a Benjaminite is called Yehudi and answers that whoever rejects idolatry is called a Jew (Bavli Megillah 13a).

a: whose name was Mordecai
p: The name is built on that of the Babylonian god Marduk. A Persian official Marduka is known from tablets.
b: Mordecai means something like "man of Marduk," the chief god of Babylon. Jews of the exile often bore local names: Daniel's friends got Babylonian names (Daniel 1:7), and Zerubbabel's name means "seed of Babylon." Tablets from Persepolis from the reign of Darius I and early Xerxes name several officials called Marduka, and one Babylonian text, first published by Arthur Ungnad, names a Marduka who was a sipir (an accountant or scribe) on a mission from Susa, late in the reign of Darius I or early in that of Xerxes. Some scholars think he may be the Mordecai of Esther; others reply that the name was common and the identification cannot be proved (Clines; Yamauchi).

a: the son of Kish, a man of Benjamin
p: Kish was the father of King Saul. Shimei was a man of Saul's clan who cursed David.
b: "There lived a Benjaminite man named Kish" (1 Samuel 9:1), the father of Saul, Israel's first king. Shimei is also the name of the Benjaminite of Saul's clan who cursed David (2 Samuel 16:5). Traditional Jewish readers took Kish and Shimei to be distant ancestors: the Talmud identifies this Shimei with the man who cursed David, and says David spared him so that Mordecai could be born (Bavli Megillah 13a; compare 1 Kings 2:8–9). Many modern readers agree that the names are meant to call up Saul, whether as real ancestors or as a family line given in shorthand. Either way the stage is set: a descendant of Kish will face a descendant of Agag (3:1), the Amalekite king Saul spared (1 Samuel 15:8–9). Others take the three names as Mordecai's father, grandfather and great-grandfather and see no deeper link.

a: who had been exiled from Jerusalem
p: Read strictly, Mordecai went into exile in 597 BC. That would make him over a hundred. The 'who' may refer to Kish.
b: Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) was taken to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12–15). If Mordecai himself was among the exiles, he would be well over a hundred by Xerxes' seventh year (2:16), and Esther, his cousin, far too old to be chosen queen. So most translators and commentators read the "who" as Kish, the last name in 2:5, or as a way of saying his family was carried off. The Hebrew allows either. Those who read the book as a historical novel see the dating as part of its storytelling; those who read it as history take the "who" as Kish. The verb "exile" (galah) comes four times in one verse, stressing that Mordecai's people live in exile.

a: Hadassah, also called Esther
p: Hadassah means 'myrtle.' Esther may come from Persian 'star' or the goddess Ishtar. The rabbis heard 'hidden.'
b: Hadassah is Hebrew for the myrtle, a fragrant evergreen used at the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8:15) and named in the prophets' pictures of renewal (Isaiah 55:13; Zechariah 1:8). Ester is probably Persian stara, "star," or a form of the Babylonian goddess's name Ishtar. Like Daniel and Mordecai, she bears a Hebrew name and a foreign one. The Talmud hears a pun on hester, "hiding": she hid her people (2:10, 20), and God "hid his face" in her days, as Deuteronomy says: "On that day I will keep my face hidden" (Deuteronomy 31:18; Bavli Chullin 139b; Bavli Megillah 13a).

a: Esther was one of those taken
p: Esther is taken into a gentile king's bed and hides her Jewishness. Readers have judged this very differently.
b: The verb is passive: Esther "was taken." Many rabbinic readers stress that she had no choice; the Talmud even says she sat "like the ground," passive, in the king's bed, and remained in her heart Mordecai's (Bavli Megillah 13b; Sanhedrin 74b), and the Greek prayer has her say she hates "the bed of the uncircumcised" (Addition C). Other readers, Jewish and Christian, note that Deuteronomy forbids marriage to foreigners (Deuteronomy 7:3) and that Esther, unlike Daniel, says nothing about food (2:9; compare Daniel 1:8); they see her as assimilated until chapter 4 wakes her. Many modern scholars argue that the book does not ask this question: it shows a Jew surviving and rising in a foreign court, as Joseph married an Egyptian priest's daughter (Genesis 41:45), and judges her by her courage when the time comes (4:16). See the chapter page.

a: she won his loyal love
p: Hesed, 'loyal love,' is God's covenant word. Here a Persian eunuch, and later the king, show it to Esther.
b: This site renders hesed as "loyal love" (see the site's terms). Elsewhere in the Bible it is above all what God shows his people (Exodus 34:6) and what people owe one another in a bond. In Esther the phrase nasa chesed lifne, "carry hesed before," means much the same as winning someone's favor (compare chen vachesed, "favor and loyal love," in 2:17); the site keeps "loyal love" so readers can see the word. In Esther it comes only from Persians, Hegai here and the king in 2:17. Where Genesis says of Joseph in prison that the LORD "showed him loyal love" (Genesis 39:21) and Daniel says God gave Daniel favor with his steward (Daniel 1:9), Esther names no giver. Many readers see here the first hint of the book's hidden God; others read it simply as Esther's charm.

a: her share of food
p: Unlike Daniel, Esther raises no objection to the king's food. The rabbis said she ate only seeds.
b: Daniel refused the king's food and wine (Daniel 1:8–16). Esther, given her "portions" by Hegai, is not said to refuse anything. The Talmud says the seven maids were chosen so that she could count the Sabbath by them, and that she lived on seeds, like Daniel (Bavli Megillah 13a). The Greek prayer has her say she never ate at Haman's table nor drank the wine of drink offerings (Addition C). The Hebrew is silent, and many modern readers think the silence is the point: here is a Jew living as the empire lived, whose loyalty is tested in another way.

a: Esther did not let anyone know which people or family she came from
p: Mordecai's order is never explained. Readers suggest caution, prudence, or strategy.
b: The book gives no reason. Caution: Jews in the empire had enemies, as chapter 3 shows, and a Jewish queen might be resented. Prudence: a girl known to be from a subject people might have been sent home or kept low. Strategy: many readers see the secret as part of the plot, kept for the moment when Esther reveals it and turns the king against Haman (7:3–4). The repetition at 2:20 makes it a theme, and her name, if it means "hidden," fits it. It also makes Mordecai's openness in 3:4 stand out: he tells everyone he is a Jew.

a: twelve months
p: Myrrh oil and perfumes were the luxuries of the ancient world. The year also kept the women apart.
b: Myrrh, a fragrant tree resin from Arabia and East Africa, was mixed with oil for perfume and skin care (Song of Songs 5:5; Psalm 45:8). The Hebrew besamim covers spices and balsam. Some readers think the long time also had a practical purpose: making sure no woman came to the king already pregnant. The numbers show the lavishness the book likes: 180 days of display (1:4), twelve months of perfume, 10,000 talents of silver (3:9).

a: the king's eunuch who kept the concubines
p: Pilagshim are secondary wives. After one night, most of these women would join them for life.
b: A concubine (pilegesh) was a wife of lower rank, with fewer rights and whose children inherited less (Genesis 25:6; Judges 19:1; 2 Samuel 5:13). These women would spend the rest of their lives in the king's household, called back only if he remembered their names. The book states the facts plainly and moves on; modern readers often feel their weight. Esther escapes this fate only because the king "loved" her (2:17).

a: She asked for nothing except what Hegai said she should take
p: Esther trusts the expert. Readers have seen modesty, wisdom, or simple good sense in this.
b: Each woman could take whatever she wanted to the king (2:13). Esther takes only what Hegai advises. Jewish tradition praises her modesty; many modern readers point out that she shows the court wisdom the book admires, listening to the person who knows the king, as she later plans her approach with care (5:4–8). Talmon reads the whole book as a "wisdom tale," in which Esther and Mordecai are wise courtiers and Haman the foolish schemer.

a: in the seventh year he was king
p: Tebeth is December to January. The seventh year of Xerxes was 479 BC, just after his war with Greece.
b: Tebeth is a Babylonian month name, used by Jews after the exile (compare Nisan in 3:7). Vashti was deposed in the third year (1:3); Esther comes to the king about four years later. Herodotus places Xerxes back at Sardis and Susa after his defeat at Plataea in 479 BC and tells of his tangled love affairs there (Histories 9.108–113). The Greek gives a different month (see the variant).

a: He gave the provinces a release
p: Hanachah means 'rest.' It may mean a holiday, a tax break or an amnesty.
b: The word is found only here. It comes from the root for "rest," the same root the book uses for the Jews' "rest" from their enemies (9:16–18, 22). Many scholars take it as a remission of taxes; the Greek has aphesis, "release" (as in a release of debts), and Herodotus says a new Persian king once granted a three-year tax remission (Histories 3.67). Others take it as a public holiday or an amnesty for prisoners.

a: The virgins were brought together a second time
p: No one is sure why the virgins are gathered again. The clause has puzzled readers since ancient times.
b: The Old Greek has no such clause here: it says only that Mordecai served in the court, and the Alpha Text has no 2:19–23 at all (see the variant). Some think the Hebrew means the king kept collecting women even after Esther was queen; others that it refers back to the first gathering (2:8), to set the time of the plot; others think a copyist repeated words from 2:8. The clause sets the scene for 2:21: the court is busy, and Mordecai is at his post in the gate.

a: sitting in the king's gate
p: To sit in the king's gate meant to hold a post at court, not just to wait outside.
b: In the ancient Near East the gate was where officials did business and judges heard cases (Ruth 4:1; 2 Samuel 19:8). Daniel served "at the king's gate" in Babylon (Daniel 2:49). The great gate building at Susa, found by the French excavations, had rooms for officials. So Mordecai is probably a minor royal official, which explains how he overhears the eunuchs (2:21) and why the king's servants in the gate expect him to bow (3:2). The Greek says plainly that he served in the court.

a: Bigthan and Teresh
p: Palace plots were real: Xerxes himself was murdered in his bedroom by court insiders in 465 BC.
b: Greek writers report that Xerxes was killed by Artabanus, the commander of his guard, with the help of a eunuch (Ctesias; Diodorus, Library 11.69). This plot fails because Mordecai overhears it. The Talmud says the two spoke in their own language, Tarsian, not knowing that Mordecai, a member of the Sanhedrin, understood it (Bavli Megillah 13b). The Old Greek tells a version of this plot twice: in Addition A, where the eunuchs are named Gabatha and Tharra, and here in chapter 2, without names but with a motive: they were aggrieved "because Mordecai had been promoted" (see the variant). The Alpha Text tells it only in Addition A, where the eunuchs are Astaos and Thedeutes. The story is placed here to pay off in 6:1–3.

a: hanged on a pole
p: Not a gallows with a rope. The Persians impaled offenders or displayed their bodies on stakes.
b: Talah 'al 'ets is "hang on a tree" or "on a pole." Herodotus says Darius impaled three thousand leading men of Babylon after a revolt (Histories 3.159), and Darius's own Behistun inscription records rebels impaled at Ecbatana. The word may mean impaling a living man or putting a dead body on display (compare Joshua 10:26; Deuteronomy 21:22–23). The traditional English "gallows" suggests a rope and a trapdoor, which is misleading. The pole returns in Haman's plans (5:14) and his end (7:10).

a: the book of the daily records
p: Persian kings kept records of service done for them. This entry will be read on a sleepless night (6:1).
b: The Hebrew is sefer divre hayyamim, "the book of the matters of the days," the same phrase used for the court records of Israel's kings and the title of Chronicles. Herodotus says Xerxes' scribes wrote down the names of men who served him well at the battle of Salamis (Histories 8.90), and rewarding a "benefactor of the king" was a Persian custom (8.85). The Jewish elders in Ezra 4:15 ask the king to search "your fathers' record book." Mordecai is not rewarded now; the delay matters in chapter 6.

a: Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite
p: 'Agagite' links Haman to Agag, king of Amalek, whom Saul son of Kish spared. Mordecai is a son of Kish.
b: Agag was the Amalekite king whom Saul captured alive instead of destroying: "Agag king of Amalek he captured alive" (1 Samuel 15:8). Samuel then "hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal" (1 Samuel 15:33). Balaam had foretold that Israel's king "will be higher than Agag" (Numbers 24:7). Jewish tradition reads Haman as an Amalekite: Josephus calls him one (Antiquities 11.209), and the Targum traces his family back to Amalek. The feud of Exodus 17:16, "The LORD will war with Amalek, one generation after another," comes to a head in Susa. Many modern scholars agree that the title is a literary signal, whether or not Haman was literally descended from Agag. A few once linked it to a place named Agag in Media, but no such place is securely known. The Greek calls him a "Bougaean" instead (see the variant).

a: He lifted him high and gave him a seat above every other official around him
p: No reason is given. Mordecai saved the king's life and got nothing; Haman gets everything.
b: The chapter opens right after Mordecai's unrewarded service (2:21–23). The contrast is pointed: the man who saved the king is forgotten, and a man who has done nothing in the story is lifted up. The writer gives Haman no merit and no history, only a family name. Readers have seen in this the arbitrary favor of a royal court, the kind of world in which the book's first readers lived. The reversal will come when the king's sleepless night brings Mordecai's deed to light (6:1–3).

a: Mordecai, however, did not go down on his knees, and he did not bow
p: The text gives only 'he was a Jew.' Readers have offered at least four explanations.
b: Israelites bowed to kings and great men without sin: "Abraham rose and bowed low to the people of the land" (Genesis 23:7), and David "bent low with his face to the earth and bowed down" to Saul (1 Samuel 24:8). So why not to Haman? 1. Worship due to God alone. The Midrash says Haman wore an idol on his clothes or claimed divine honor (Esther Rabbah 7:5; compare Bavli Sanhedrin 61b), and in the Greek prayer Mordecai says he would not set a man's glory above God's (Addition C). 2. Persian prostration. Greeks refused proskynesis before Persian kings as fit only for gods (Herodotus, Histories 7.136), and some think Jews felt the same. 3. The ancient feud. A Benjaminite of Kish's line would not bow to an Agagite (Targum Sheni; many modern readers, among them Fox and Levenson; see the chapter page). 4. Pride or stubbornness. Some readers, ancient and modern, think the book does not wholly approve: Mordecai's stand endangers every Jew. The text's only reason, "he was a Jew" (3:4), leaves room for all four.

a: Day after day they spoke to him, but he would not listen to them
t: 'Day after day ... he would not listen'
p: The words echo Joseph refusing Potiphar's wife. Mordecai, like Joseph, says no to the powerful.
b: The Hebrew matches Genesis 39:10: "She spoke to Joseph day after day, but he would not listen to her." Joseph's refusal landed him in prison; Mordecai's will put his people under a death sentence. Both men are Hebrews at a foreign court whose faithfulness is tested in a small daily matter, and both are raised in the end. This is one of the clearest of the many Joseph echoes in Esther (see 2:3). The Hebrew has a small spelling difference here (written "when they spoke," read "as they spoke"), which does not change the sense.

a: He had explained to them that he was a Jew
p: The only reason Mordecai gives is who he is. That makes the quarrel about a people, not one man.
b: "Mordecai's reasons" (literally "words") may mean his excuse, or simply his behavior. The servants want to know if Haman will accept it. By giving his people as his reason, Mordecai turns a court quarrel into a matter of identity, and Haman takes it that way (3:6). The contrast with Esther, who at the same time is hiding her people (2:20), is part of the story's design.

a: Haman set out to annihilate every Jew in Ahasuerus's entire kingdom
t: From one man to a whole people
p: Haman's answer to one man's insult is to destroy a whole people. The book makes this the pattern of hatred against Jews.
b: Haman thinks Mordecai alone too small a target. The plan is genocide: the verb hashmid, "annihilate," means to wipe out entirely. Readers have long seen in Haman a type of the enemies of the Jews in every age; Purim is kept partly to remember that such plans have been made and defeated. The irony is that the Amalekite, whose memory Israel was to "wipe out" (Deuteronomy 25:19), now plans to wipe out Israel. Christian readers note that the hatred is directed at the people as such, not at any crime they have done.

a: Pur, that is, the lot, was thrown
p: Pur is an Akkadian word for a lot. An Assyrian clay die called a puru has been found.
b: The book explains the foreign word for its Hebrew readers: "Pur, that is, the lot" (goral). Akkadian puru means a lot or a share. A small inscribed clay cube from Assyria, the "die of Iahali," an official of Shalmaneser III (800s BC), calls itself a puru and prays that his year in office will be prosperous. Babylonians and Persians cast lots to find lucky days. Israel too used lots, trusting God for the result (Leviticus 16:8; Proverbs 16:33). Haman's lot, cast to doom the Jews, gives its name to the feast that celebrates their rescue: Purim (9:24–26).

a: In the first month, Nisan
t: Lots cast in the month of Passover
p: Haman casts lots in the month of Israel's great rescue from Egypt.
b: Nisan is the month of Passover (Exodus 12:2; Leviticus 23:5). The decree is written on the thirteenth of Nisan (3:12), the day before Passover, and Esther's three-day fast (4:16) would fall over the feast. Readers have long noticed the timing: the new threat comes in the month that remembers the Exodus, and the story ends with a new feast of rescue. In Babylonian belief the gods fixed the destinies of the coming year at the New Year festival in Nisan, which some think explains why Haman cast his lots then.

a: down to the twelfth month, the month of Adar
p: The lot fell almost a year away. The Talmud says Haman rejoiced because Moses died in Adar.
b: The Talmud says that when the lot fell on Adar, Haman was glad, because Moses died in that month; but he did not know that Moses was also born in it (Bavli Megillah 13b). The long wait, eleven months, matters to the story: it gives time for Esther to act and for a second decree to reach the provinces (8:9–12). Readers who see God's hand in the book often point to this delay as the first sign of it, since, as Proverbs says, the lot is thrown into the lap, but the whole verdict comes from the LORD (Proverbs 16:33).

a: One people lives scattered here and there, kept apart
p: Haman mixes truth and lies: the Jews are scattered and keep their own laws, but they are not disloyal.
b: Haman does not name the people. The words are true in part: the Jews were "scattered" (Deuteronomy 4:27: "The LORD will scatter you among the peoples") and kept laws unlike others'. The lie is that they "do not obey" the king's laws; the only Jew in the story who has disobeyed is Mordecai, and he has just saved the king's life (2:21–23). Later writers made the same charge: Greek and Roman authors accused the Jews of hating other peoples and living apart (Tacitus, Histories 5.5; Josephus answers such charges in Against Apion). Many readers see in Haman's speech the first full statement of anti-Jewish prejudice, and the book's answer to it. Haman also turns to money (3:9).
orig: עַם־אֶחָד מְפֻזָּר וּמְפֹרָד (am echad mefuzzar umeforad)

a: 10,000 talents of silver
p: 10,000 talents is roughly 300 to 340 tons of silver, more than half a year's income for the whole empire.
b: A talent weighed about 30 to 34 kilograms (66 to 75 pounds), so the sum is roughly 300 to 340 metric tons of silver. Herodotus lists the yearly tribute of the Persian provinces as about 14,560 talents (Histories 3.95), so Haman offers more than half the empire's annual revenue, perhaps from the plunder of the Jews (3:13). Whether the king accepts it is unclear (3:11). The Talmud says God, knowing Haman would weigh out silver against Israel, had Israel give their half-shekels first (Exodus 30:13) to outweigh it (Bavli Megillah 13b).

a: The king slipped the signet ring off his hand
p: The signet ring was the king's signature. Pharaoh gave his to Joseph; this king gives his to Haman.
b: A signet ring carried the owner's seal, pressed into clay or wax to sign documents (compare 1 Kings 21:8). The wording echoes Genesis 41:42: "Pharaoh slipped the signet ring off his own hand and set it on Joseph's hand." Here the king hands his power to the enemy; in 8:2 the same ring goes to Mordecai. The Old Greek has no "enemy of the Jews" here: the king gives the ring "to seal against the Jews" (see the variant). The Talmud says that the taking off of this ring did more to bring Israel back to God than forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses (Bavli Megillah 14a).

a: the enemy of the Jews
p: Tsorer hayyehudim becomes Haman's title. It comes four times in the book.
b: The title (3:10; 8:1; 9:10, 24) is spoken by the narrator, never by the king, who does not yet know that his queen is one of the Jews. It joins "the Agagite" to define Haman entirely by his enmity. The Old Greek leaves it out here (see the variant at "the enemy of the Jews"). At the Purim reading the congregation often drowns out his name with noise.

a: The silver is yours
t: Does the king refuse the money?
p: It can mean 'Keep your money' or 'The money is given to you.' Later verses suggest a sale.
b: The Hebrew is "the silver is given to you." Many read it as a polite refusal: keep the money. But Mordecai later reports "the precise figure of the silver Haman had said he would weigh out" (4:7), and Esther later says that she and her people have been sold (7:4). So others take the king's words as the courteous phrasing of a deal, like Ephron's "I give it to you" while naming his price (Genesis 23:11–15). Either way, the king hands over a whole people without asking who they are.

a: during the first month, on its thirteenth day
p: The decree goes out the day before Passover, set for the thirteenth day of another month.
b: The decree is dated the thirteenth of Nisan and sets the killing for the thirteenth of Adar (3:13), eleven months later. The Talmud links this to Esther's fast: three days from the fourteenth to the sixteenth of Nisan, so the Jews fasted through Passover (Bavli Megillah 15a; see 4:17). The empire's administration is on show: scribes, satraps, governors and officials, every script and every language, all sealed with the king's ring.

a: to annihilate, kill and destroy every Jew
p: The triple command echoes Saul's orders against Amalek. It will be turned around in chapter 8.
b: "Annihilate, kill and destroy" piles up three verbs for one act, in the style of a legal decree. The list of victims, "from the young to the old, little children and women," recalls Samuel's command to Saul against Amalek: "Put to death man and woman, child and nursing baby" (1 Samuel 15:3). Now an Agagite gives that order against Israel. The Hebrew names the day, the thirteenth of Adar; the Old Greek and the Alpha Text say only "on one day of the twelfth month," and only Addition B gives a number, the fourteenth. The second decree uses the same three verbs, word for word, for the Jews' right to defend themselves (8:11); see 8:11 and chapter 9 on how that is carried out.

a: Runners carried the letters
p: The Persian empire had a famous express post, with riders and relay stations along royal roads.
b: Herodotus admired the Persian messengers: riders posted a day's journey apart passed messages from one to the next, and "neither snow nor rain nor heat nor night" stopped them (Histories 8.98). Tablets from Persepolis record food rations given to travelers carrying sealed royal documents. The Royal Road from Susa to Sardis ran about 1,600 miles. An order from Susa could reach the far provinces within weeks, so the eleven months before Adar left plenty of time.

a: Then the king and Haman sat down to drink
p: The king and Haman drink while a people is condemned, as Joseph's brothers ate after throwing him in the pit.
b: The picture recalls Genesis 37:25: after throwing Joseph into the pit, "they sat down to eat their meal." The book's feasts here turn dark: the empire's machinery runs, and its rulers relax. The next words, "the city of Susa was in turmoil," say that ordinary people, not only Jews, were shocked. Some readers see a hint that Haman's hatred was not shared by the empire's subjects.

a: the city of Susa was in turmoil
p: Navokhah means perplexed or thrown into confusion. Susa does not understand the decree either.
b: The verb is used of the Israelites wandering lost in the wilderness (Exodus 14:3) and of herds milling about without pasture (Joel 1:18). The city's confusion matches the senselessness of the order. When Mordecai triumphs, the same city shouts for joy (8:15). The contrast frames the whole middle of the book.

a: dressed himself in sackcloth and ashes
p: Coarse goat-hair cloth and ashes were the signs of grief, repentance and plea.
b: Sackcloth was rough cloth of goat or camel hair. Mourners tore their clothes, wore sackcloth and put dust or ashes on their heads: Jacob, for Joseph, "tore his clothing and wrapped sackcloth around his hips" (Genesis 37:34). The same acts went with fasting and prayer for rescue, as at Nineveh (Jonah 3:5–8) and in Daniel's prayer (Daniel 9:3). Mordecai's public mourning is both grief and protest. It is also, in the book's language, as close as it comes to prayer: no one in Esther speaks to God.

a: letting out a loud, bitter cry
p: The phrase echoes Esau's cry when Jacob took his blessing. The Midrash says Mordecai paid for it.
b: When Esau found the blessing gone, "he cried out with a cry, a great and bitter cry beyond measure" (Genesis 27:34). Here Mordecai "cried out a cry, loud and bitter." The Midrash notes the match and says that the cry Jacob caused Esau was repaid in Susa, when a descendant of Jacob cried out because of Haman, a descendant of Esau through Amalek (Genesis Rabbah 67:4; compare Genesis 36:12). The Greek adds what Mordecai cried (see the variant).

a: They fasted, wept and cried aloud
t: Fasting without a word about God
p: The Jews fast, weep and wail. The Hebrew never says they prayed. The Greek adds prayers.
b: Fasting in the Bible goes with prayer: "fasting and praying before the God of the heavens" (Nehemiah 1:4), Ezra's fast to "ask him for a straight road" (Ezra 8:21), and Joel's call to come back to God with fasting and tears (Joel 2:12). Esther names the fasting and the mourning and leaves out the God they would have prayed to. Most Jewish and Christian readers assume prayer was part of it and see the silence as the book's way of keeping God hidden. Some critical scholars think the writer deliberately kept religion out of a festival story. The Greek fills the gap with the prayers of Mordecai and Esther (Addition C, after 4:17).

a: the queen was in anguish
p: Vattitchalchal is a strong word, used of the pains of labor.
b: The verb comes from the root of a woman's labor pains (Isaiah 26:17; Jeremiah 4:31). Esther does not yet know what has happened; she sees only Mordecai in sackcloth. Her first act, sending him clothes, may be care for him, or an attempt to get him back into the gate where he could talk to her. His refusal says that what has happened cannot be covered up.

a: Hathach
p: A minor eunuch carries the book's most important messages. The rabbis said he was Daniel.
b: Hathach is the go-between for the whole exchange of 4:5–12. The Talmud identifies him with Daniel, explaining the name from chatakh, "cut": Daniel had been "cut down" from his high rank, or matters of state were "decided" by him (Bavli Megillah 15a). The legend reflects the wish to see the great Jews of the exile working together. The Hebrew says only that he was one of the king's eunuchs, assigned to serve the queen. The Old Greek calls him Achrathaios.

a: the precise figure of the silver
p: Mordecai knows the exact sum Haman offered. He has an insider's knowledge of the court.
b: Parashat hakkesef means "the exact statement of the silver" (the word appears again in 10:2 for an exact account). How Mordecai knows a private offer made to the king is not said, but it fits a man with a post in the gate (2:19). By giving the figure, Mordecai shows Esther that this is not a rumor but a bought decree.

a: make her request to him for her people
p: For the first time Esther's people are named as hers, the people she has been hiding (2:10, 20).
b: Mordecai's charge uses two verbs: hitchannen, "plead for grace," and bikkesh, "make a request." The words "for her people" undo the secret Mordecai himself imposed (2:10, 20). To plead for her people Esther must reveal that she belongs to them, which she will do in 7:3–4. The Greek adds that she should remember her humble beginnings and call upon the Lord (see the variant).

a: one law applies, and that is death
t: No one comes to the king uncalled
p: Greek writers describe the guarded Persian court. Reliefs from Persepolis show the king receiving visitors.
b: Herodotus says that the Median king Deioces first ruled that no one should come into the king's presence; all business went through messengers (Histories 1.99). When Intaphernes, one of the seven nobles with the right of entry, forced his way in, Darius suspected a plot and put him and most of his family to death (3.118–119). Reliefs from the Treasury at Persepolis show the enthroned king, staff or scepter in hand, receiving an official who bows with his hand to his mouth. The book adds that the king could spare an uninvited visitor by holding out his gold scepter. Some readers note that a request for an audience could be sent, which Esther does not seem to consider; others reply that a queen who had not been called for thirty days could not count on it.

a: no one has called me in to the king for thirty days now
p: Esther's last words hint that she has fallen out of favor. Her fear is real.
b: Esther does not refuse; she explains. A month without a summons suggests the king's interest has cooled, and Vashti's fate shows what happens to a queen who displeases him (1:19). Some readers hear reluctance or self-protection; others hear plain realism. The exchange that follows turns on whether she will put her safety ahead of her people.

a: Don't tell yourself that living in the king's house will let you escape when the rest of the Jews do not
p: Mordecai tells Esther the palace will not save her. Is he warning her or threatening her?
b: Most readers hear a warning: the decree covers "every Jew" (3:13), and her identity will come out. Some hear something harder in 4:14: if she stays silent, "you and the house of your father perish," as if her silence will bring its own punishment, from God or from the Jews who survive. The Hebrew allows both. Either way, Mordecai answers her fear with a deeper danger: to save herself she would have to give up her people.

a: relief and rescue will spring up for the Jews from somewhere else
p: Is 'another place' a hidden way of naming God? Readers have argued about this for two thousand years.
b: God, veiled. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, hear a reference to God, as close as the book comes to naming him. Later rabbinic Hebrew calls God HaMakom, "the Place," Josephus makes the help explicitly God's: Mordecai says God would surely help the Jews in some other way (Antiquities 11.227), and the Targum names "the Lord of the world." A human helper. Others, among them Fox, argue that "another place" means some other person or power, since the parallel "you and the house of your father" is human; on this view Mordecai is confident the Jews will survive but does not say how. Deliberately open. Many modern readers think the ambiguity is the point: the book will not name God, but it leaves room for faith. The Greek has "help and protection will come to the Jews from elsewhere."

a: And who knows?
p: 'Who knows' is the Bible's phrase for humble hope: God may act, but no one can be sure.
b: David fasted for his dying son because, he said, "'Who knows? The LORD might show me favor, and the boy would live'" (2 Samuel 12:22). Joel 2:14 and Jonah 3:9 use the same words of whether God will turn from his anger. Mordecai's "who knows" belongs to that family: not certainty, but enough hope to act on.

a: Perhaps it was for a time like this that you came to royal power
p: The book's most famous line. It suggests that Esther's rise was not an accident.
b: Literally: "and who knows whether for a time like this you reached royalty?" Everything in chapters 1–2 that seemed like chance or royal whim, Vashti's fall, the beauty search, Esther's favor, now looks like preparation. Jewish and Christian readers have taken it as the key to the book's view of providence: God works through events, choices and timing, even when he is not named (compare Joseph's words, Genesis 50:20, "You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good"). Some critical readers see a more modest claim: Esther's position gives her a duty. The verse is often quoted to call people to act at a decisive moment.
orig: וּמִי יוֹדֵעַ אִם־לְעֵת כָּזֹאת הִגַּעַתְּ לַמַּלְכוּת

a: fast on my behalf
p: A three-day fast for the queen. Jews keep the 'Fast of Esther' on the day before Purim.
b: Esther's command is the turning point: the queen who obeyed Mordecai (2:20) now gives the orders, and he obeys her (4:17). The fast is total, no food or drink, "night and day." Fasting in the Bible is a plea to God (Ezra 8:21; Jonah 3:7–9), so most readers take it as an unspoken prayer. Jews keep the Fast of Esther on the thirteenth of Adar, the day before Purim, a custom that takes its name from this verse, though the date comes from 9:31 and the day of battle (9:1). If the fast began on the day the decree was issued, it fell over Passover (3:12; Bavli Megillah 15a).

a: which the law does not allow
p: Esther will break the Persian law to save her people. The book's word for law, dat, appears again.
b: The empire's "law" (dat, see 1:8) has threatened the Jews (3:14) and keeps the king out of reach (4:11). Now Esther chooses to go in against the law. Readers note the contrast with Vashti, who broke protocol by refusing to come (1:12); Esther breaks it by coming unasked.

a: And if I perish, I perish
p: Esther's words echo Jacob letting Benjamin go: 'if I am bereaved, I am bereaved.'
b: The Hebrew pattern "as I perish, I perish" matches Jacob's words when he sent Benjamin to Egypt: "As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved" (Genesis 43:14). Esther, of the tribe of Benjamin, accepts the risk as Jacob did. Some readers hear resignation; most hear resolve: she has decided, and the outcome is no longer hers to control. The verb "perish" picks up Mordecai's warning in 4:14.

a: Mordecai went his way
p: The verb can mean 'passed' or 'crossed.' The rabbis read it as 'he transgressed' by fasting on Passover.
b: Vayya'avor usually means "went on" or "crossed over." The Talmud gives two readings: Mordecai "crossed" a stream to gather the Jews, or he "transgressed," fasting on the first day of Passover, since the fast ran from the fourteenth to the sixteenth of Nisan (Bavli Megillah 15a; see 3:12). Either way the roles have reversed: Mordecai now does "all that Esther had commanded him," as she once did all he said (2:20). Gerleman argued that Esther retells the Exodus story throughout, and the Passover timing is one of his strongest points. The Greek inserts the prayers of Mordecai and Esther here (see the variant).
